items.prompt: An S3 bucket must protect against accidental overwrites and deletions, while operators still need to recover a prior object version. Which design is appropriate?
constraints: The bucket stores versioned business objects.
Accidental deletes are a realistic failure mode.
Recovery must be possible without restoring a whole backup.

options.text: Enable S3 Versioning and define lifecycle handling for noncurrent versions; treat a delete marker as a versioned state that can be removed to expose a prior version.
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration because it preserves every previous object version after a delete.
Use a security group because S3 object deletes are controlled by subnet state.
Use S3 replication only because replication replaces versioning in the source bucket.

feedback.Reason: S3 Versioning keeps multiple object versions and makes accidental overwrites or deletes recoverable at the object level.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A delete in a versioned bucket normally creates a delete marker instead of removing the prior version. Noncurrent versions remain subject to lifecycle policy.
Details.scenarioApplication: The operations runbook restores a prior version or removes an accidental delete marker and separately controls storage growth from old versions.
Details.errorCorrection: Transfer Acceleration is a transfer optimization, security groups do not authorize S3 objects, and replication does not replace source versioning.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Versioning improves recovery but can increase storage cost unless noncurrent versions are retained or expired deliberately.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Transfer Acceleration changes transfer paths and does not preserve object versions.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Security groups are network controls and do not manage S3 object version history.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Replication can create another copy, but source-bucket versioning still governs the source object history.

items.prompt: A data set is frequently read for 30 days, rarely read for the next year, and must remain available without application changes. Which control matches the lifecycle requirement?
constraints: The objects remain in the same S3 bucket.
The access pattern changes predictably over time.
The team wants managed storage-class movement.

options.text: Use an S3 Lifecycle rule with age-based transitions to an appropriate lower-cost storage class, after validating retrieval and minimum-storage-duration constraints.
Use an IAM policy that automatically changes an object’s storage class whenever a user reads it.
Delete the objects after 30 days and rely on CloudTrail to reconstruct their contents later.
Move all objects to S3 One Zone-IA without considering access frequency or resilience requirements.

feedback.Reason: S3 Lifecycle rules express age-based transitions while keeping the object address stable.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Lifecycle actions can transition objects between S3 storage classes. The selected class must fit access frequency, availability, retrieval, and minimum-duration requirements.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner models reads and retrieval time, then implements and monitors transitions rather than tying storage class to individual callers.
Details.errorCorrection: IAM authorizes actions but does not schedule storage-class changes, CloudTrail is not a content backup, and One Zone-IA is not a universal choice.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Lower-cost classes can impose retrieval charges or minimum storage durations, so lifecycle rules must reflect the actual retention and access profile.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: IAM policies do not implement time-based S3 storage-class transitions.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: CloudTrail records API activity and cannot reconstruct deleted object contents.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: One Zone-IA changes resilience and cost characteristics and must not be selected without those constraints.

items.prompt: A temporary export must be retained for 90 days and then removed, but the bucket also contains regulated records. How should expiration be scoped?
constraints: The temporary export has a dedicated prefix or tag.
Regulated records have a longer retention requirement.
Deletion must be automated and auditable.

options.text: Apply an S3 Lifecycle expiration rule only to the export prefix or tag, and exclude records whose retention policy is longer or legally protected.
Set one bucket-wide 90-day expiration because lifecycle rules cannot target a prefix or tag.
Use an S3 bucket policy Deny on GetObject because denying reads deletes objects after the retention period.
Use CloudWatch alarms to delete all objects when the bucket reaches a size threshold.

feedback.Reason: Lifecycle expiration should target the data class that is actually disposable, not a bucket-wide population with different retention obligations.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: S3 Lifecycle rules can be filtered by object key prefix or tags and can expire current or noncurrent versions according to the rule.
Details.scenarioApplication: The data owner tags temporary exports, reviews the rule against protected prefixes, and monitors expiration actions as part of retention evidence.
Details.errorCorrection: Bucket-wide deletion ignores classification, policy Deny blocks access rather than deleting, and size alarms do not express retention dates.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Automated deletion reduces storage cost but becomes a governance control that must be tested against legal holds, versions, and restore needs.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A bucket can contain objects with different lifecycle filters; a single global expiration would violate the longer retention class.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A bucket policy controls authorization and does not expire objects.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Bucket size is not a retention criterion and a CloudWatch alarm is not an object lifecycle rule.

items.prompt: A records team needs WORM retention, but a specifically authorized compliance role must be able to shorten a retention period during an approved correction. Which S3 Object Lock mode fits?
constraints: The bucket uses Versioning.
Most users must not overwrite or delete retained versions.
An authorized override process exists.

options.text: Use S3 Object Lock Governance mode and restrict the permissions that allow authorized users to bypass governance retention.
Use Compliance mode because it permits any administrator to shorten retention when a ticket is approved.
Use S3 Lifecycle expiration alone because lifecycle rules are immutable WORM controls.
Use an S3 bucket ACL because ACLs create a retention period on every object version.

feedback.Reason: Governance mode provides WORM retention while allowing a tightly controlled permission path to bypass retention.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Governance mode prevents most users from altering protected versions, while users with the required bypass permissions can override it. Object Lock depends on Versioning.
Details.scenarioApplication: Security separates ordinary writers from the narrow bypass role, logs bypass operations, and validates the approval process.
Details.errorCorrection: Compliance mode is designed to prevent deletion or shortening even by privileged users, lifecycle is not an override-controlled WORM mode, and ACLs are not retention controls.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Governance mode supports operational correction but requires strict control of bypass permissions; it is weaker than Compliance mode against privileged override.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Compliance mode is intended to prevent retention shortening or deletion during the retention period.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Lifecycle expiration manages object age and does not provide the Object Lock retention model.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: ACLs authorize access and do not create WORM retention periods.

items.prompt: A regulated archive must not be deleted or have retention shortened by any user, including the account root user, during the mandated retention period. Which control is intended for this requirement?
constraints: The archive must be WORM.
Retention cannot be shortened after it is applied.
The bucket can use versioned objects.

options.text: Use S3 Object Lock Compliance mode with a retention period that meets the regulation, and govern retention configuration separately.
Use S3 Object Lock Governance mode and give the root user the bypass permission for emergency use.
Use an S3 lifecycle expiration rule because any lifecycle expiration is stronger than Object Lock.
Use SSE-KMS because encryption prevents a user with delete permission from deleting an object version.

feedback.Reason: Compliance mode is the S3 Object Lock choice when no principal should be able to shorten retention or delete a protected version during retention.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Object Lock Compliance mode prevents protected object versions from being overwritten or deleted by any user during the retention period. Versioning is required.
Details.scenarioApplication: The archive owner validates the retention duration before applying it and treats the lock as a regulatory control, not merely as an operator preference.
Details.errorCorrection: Governance mode permits an authorized bypass, lifecycle is not a WORM substitute, and encryption protects content confidentiality rather than delete authorization.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Compliance mode provides stronger immutability but makes retention mistakes difficult or impossible to correct, so policy approval must precede activation.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Governance mode is designed to permit a controlled bypass and therefore does not meet the stated no-bypass requirement.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Lifecycle expiration is an automated management action, not the Object Lock immutability guarantee.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Encryption does not prevent an authorized S3 delete operation.

items.prompt: A litigation hold applies to selected S3 records, but the end date is unknown. What should the records team use for those object versions?
constraints: The hold applies to selected objects only.
The hold duration is not known yet.
Normal retention rules remain for unrelated objects.

options.text: Apply an S3 Object Lock legal hold to the selected object versions and remove it only when the authorized legal process releases the records.
Set a one-day Object Lock retention period because a legal hold cannot outlive a numeric retention period.
Add a Deny statement to the IAM policy because IAM denies automatically create object-level legal holds.
Move the objects to S3 Standard because storage class determines whether a litigation hold exists.

feedback.Reason: An S3 legal hold protects a selected object version without requiring a predetermined retention end date.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A legal hold is independent of a retention period and prevents deletion or overwrite while active. Object Lock and Versioning provide the surrounding model.
Details.scenarioApplication: Legal operations identify the exact versions, apply the hold, record authorization, and release it only after the matter is resolved.
Details.errorCorrection: A short numeric retention does not express an unknown legal duration, IAM Deny is not a legal-hold object state, and storage class is unrelated.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Legal holds can keep data indefinitely and therefore need explicit ownership and release evidence to avoid uncontrolled retention growth.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A one-day retention does not protect a record for an unknown litigation period.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: IAM authorization and S3 Object Lock legal-hold state are different mechanisms.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: S3 storage class affects storage behavior and cost, not legal-hold state.

items.prompt: A large S3 data set has unpredictable access patterns and must remain available immediately, but the owner wants automatic cost optimization. Which option should be evaluated?
constraints: Access frequency is not predictable.
The application expects online object access.
The owner accepts monitoring and tiering charges.

options.text: Evaluate S3 Intelligent-Tiering, including its monitoring fee and eligible access tiers, for automatic movement based on changing access patterns.
Use S3 Glacier Deep Archive because unpredictable access always means the lowest storage price is the correct requirement.
Use an IAM role that changes every object to Standard-IA after its first read.
Disable lifecycle management because automatic tiering is available only for EBS volumes.

feedback.Reason: S3 Intelligent-Tiering is designed for data with changing or unknown access patterns while retaining online access characteristics.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Intelligent-Tiering monitors access and moves eligible objects among access tiers. It has monitoring and automation costs and does not make every retrieval free.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner compares object size, access latency, retention, and tier fees before enabling the class and measures actual savings.
Details.errorCorrection: Deep Archive trades retrieval latency and cost for low storage price, IAM roles do not schedule storage classes, and Intelligent-Tiering is an S3 feature.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Automatic optimization reduces manual rules but adds monitoring charges and does not remove the need to choose an appropriate archive or resilience model.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Deep Archive is intended for rarely accessed archive data and conflicts with the immediate-online-access constraint.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: An IAM role grants actions; it does not implement object-age or access-driven storage transitions.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Intelligent-Tiering is an S3 storage class and does not depend on EBS lifecycle management.

items.prompt: An existing Amazon S3 Glacier vault must enforce a policy-based retention period for archive records so the vault policy cannot be changed after approval. Which feature matches?
constraints: The archive is stored in a Glacier vault.
The retention policy must be locked.
The organization accepts an irreversible lock after the review window.

options.text: Use Amazon S3 Glacier Vault Lock: install the policy, review it during the in-progress period, and complete the lock only after validation.
Use an S3 bucket lifecycle rule because lifecycle rules lock an Amazon Glacier vault policy automatically.
Use a security group because archive vault policies are network ACLs in disguise.
Use a CloudWatch alarm that denies all archive deletions without changing the vault policy.

feedback.Reason: Glacier Vault Lock is the service feature for enforcing compliance controls through a locked vault access policy.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Vault Lock provides an in-progress policy state for testing and a locked state that prevents policy changes, supporting compliance retention controls.
Details.scenarioApplication: The archive owner tests retrieval and deletion behavior during the review period, obtains approval, and then completes the irreversible lock.
Details.errorCorrection: S3 Lifecycle applies to S3 objects, security groups control traffic, and alarms can signal events but do not lock a Glacier vault policy.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The completed lock is intentionally difficult to reverse, so policy errors must be found before completion and recovery procedures must be documented.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: S3 Lifecycle rules do not lock an Amazon S3 Glacier vault access policy.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Security groups are VPC network controls and are unrelated to Glacier vault policy immutability.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A CloudWatch alarm can notify but cannot enforce the vault policy or deny archive operations by itself.

items.prompt: A central backup vault must prevent protected recovery points from being deleted before the organization’s retention period expires. Which AWS Backup control should be evaluated?
constraints: Backups are managed by AWS Backup.
The vault contains protected recovery points.
The policy must cover accidental or malicious deletion.

options.text: Configure AWS Backup Vault Lock with the required retention bounds and validate the grace period and compliance behavior before relying on it.
Use an IAM Allow policy for DeleteRecoveryPoint because an Allow policy makes deletion auditable and therefore immutable.
Use an S3 Object Lock rule on the backup vault because every AWS Backup vault is an S3 bucket.
Use a security group to block the AWS Backup service from reaching the vault over the network.

feedback.Reason: AWS Backup Vault Lock is the service-native control for enforcing retention of recovery points in a backup vault.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Vault Lock can impose minimum and maximum retention behavior and provides a grace period before the lock becomes immutable according to the configured mode.
Details.scenarioApplication: The backup owner tests restore and deletion workflows, verifies the retention bounds, and documents who can administer the vault without treating IAM alone as immutability.
Details.errorCorrection: An IAM Allow enables an action rather than preventing it, backup vaults are not simply S3 buckets for Object Lock configuration, and security groups do not govern vault API retention.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Vault Lock protects recovery points but can constrain legitimate cleanup and therefore requires retention design and restore testing first.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: An Allow policy grants deletion and cannot make recovery points immutable.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: AWS Backup vault retention is governed by AWS Backup controls, not by attaching S3 Object Lock to the vault.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Network controls do not replace the AWS Backup vault’s resource and retention controls.

items.prompt: The organization requires daily backups, a weekly recovery point, and automatic expiration after the approved retention period. Where should the policy be expressed?
constraints: Resources are tagged by backup policy.
Backup frequency and retention differ by resource class.
The process should not depend on operators starting backups manually.

options.text: Use AWS Backup plans with rules for schedules and lifecycle retention, assign resources through tags or supported resource selections, and monitor plan compliance.
Use an S3 Lifecycle rule for every resource because AWS Backup plans cannot express schedules or retention.
Use a security group with a weekly rule because backup frequency is a network property.
Use only CloudTrail event history because it retains a restorable copy of each resource.

feedback.Reason: AWS Backup plans combine scheduled backup rules, lifecycle retention, and resource assignment for managed backup operations.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A backup plan can contain rules with schedules and lifecycle transitions or expiration, and resource selections can target supported resources through tags or explicit selections.
Details.scenarioApplication: The platform maps each data class to a plan, verifies that tagged resources are covered, and checks backup and restore outcomes.
Details.errorCorrection: S3 lifecycle controls S3 objects only, security groups do not schedule backups, and CloudTrail history is audit evidence rather than a backup copy.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Central plans improve consistency but require coverage monitoring, supported-resource checks, and retention choices that balance cost with recovery objectives.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: S3 Lifecycle does not schedule backups for databases, volumes, or other AWS Backup resources.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Security groups control network traffic and do not create backup schedules.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: CloudTrail event history records activity but does not provide a restorable resource backup.

items.prompt: A DynamoDB workload needs recovery to a point in time within the service-supported recovery window, without operators managing periodic snapshots. Which feature is the closest fit?
constraints: The table is supported for the feature.
Recovery must cover accidental writes between scheduled backups.
The team accepts the feature’s defined recovery window and cost.

options.text: Enable DynamoDB point-in-time recovery and verify the table’s recovery status and operational restore procedure.
Enable DynamoDB Streams because a stream is automatically a full historical table backup for any point in time.
Use an IAM policy with a Deny on PutItem because denying writes preserves all prior table states.
Use S3 Lifecycle expiration because DynamoDB tables are managed as S3 objects.

feedback.Reason: DynamoDB point-in-time recovery provides continuous backups for restoring a table to a selected point in the supported window.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: PITR continuously backs up table data and supports restore to a point in time within the configured service window; it does not mean the original table is rolled back in place.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner enables PITR, tests restore into a new table, and documents how applications switch to the restored table after validation.
Details.errorCorrection: Streams capture item-level change events for integrations, Deny prevents writes rather than preserving history, and S3 lifecycle does not manage DynamoDB tables.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: PITR reduces backup scheduling effort but has a bounded recovery window and restore operations require capacity, validation, and cutover planning.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: DynamoDB Streams are change data for consumers and are not the table’s PITR backup mechanism.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A write Deny prevents changes but does not provide recovery from an already-corrupted table.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: DynamoDB is not governed by S3 object lifecycle rules.

items.prompt: An RDS database needs automated backups and point-in-time restore for a defined operational window, while the team separately plans long-term copies. Which configuration addresses the first requirement?
constraints: The database runs on Amazon RDS.
The operational window is within the service’s automated-backup limits.
Long-term retention is a separate governance decision.

options.text: Configure the RDS automated-backup retention period and verify the backup window, then use snapshots or AWS Backup for the separate long-term requirement.
Set the database security group to retain backups because network rules determine the RDS backup window.
Disable automated backups and rely on CloudWatch metrics because metrics can restore a database to any timestamp.
Use an S3 object lifecycle rule directly on the RDS instance because RDS backups are ordinary S3 objects owned by the customer.

feedback.Reason: RDS automated backups provide the managed operational backup and point-in-time recovery window; long-term retention needs an additional copy strategy.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: RDS automated backups are retained for the configured period and support point-in-time restore within that period. Manual snapshots and backup services address different retention needs.
Details.scenarioApplication: The database owner sets retention and backup windows, tests a restore, and documents how long-term snapshots or cross-Region copies are governed.
Details.errorCorrection: Security groups do not retain backups, metrics are not restorable database state, and customers do not manage RDS automated backups through a direct S3 lifecycle rule.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Increasing automated retention improves operational recovery but does not by itself provide an independently governed long-term or cross-account copy.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Security groups govern network reachability and do not configure RDS backup retention.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: CloudWatch metrics cannot restore database data to an arbitrary timestamp.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: RDS automated backup storage is service-managed and is not configured as ordinary customer-managed S3 objects.

items.prompt: An EFS file system contains active and infrequently accessed files. The application should continue using the same file system while cold files move to a lower-cost class. Which control should be used?
constraints: The file system remains mounted by applications.
The access pattern is measurable over time.
The owner accepts file-system lifecycle transition behavior.

options.text: Configure EFS Lifecycle Management with an appropriate transition policy and validate that the file-system throughput and access characteristics meet the workload needs.
Use S3 Object Lock because EFS files are automatically stored as S3 object versions.
Use an IAM permissions boundary because boundaries move files between EFS storage classes.
Delete cold files after 30 days because EFS cannot retain data in a lower-cost storage class.

feedback.Reason: EFS Lifecycle Management moves files between EFS storage classes based on access behavior while preserving the file-system namespace.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: EFS lifecycle policies transition files into an infrequent-access or archive class according to the configured policy and access state.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner selects transition settings, measures access and retrieval behavior, and confirms the storage class and throughput mode fit the workload.
Details.errorCorrection: EFS is not an S3 versioned object store, permissions boundaries govern IAM capabilities, and lifecycle transition is not deletion.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Lower-cost EFS classes can have access charges or performance implications, so lifecycle settings must be tested against the real file workload.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: S3 Object Lock applies to S3 object versions and does not configure EFS lifecycle transitions.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: IAM permissions boundaries cap role permissions and do not move EFS files between storage classes.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: EFS supports lifecycle transitions; deleting cold files would violate the stated retention requirement.

items.prompt: A managed FSx file system needs automatic daily backups retained for 35 days, with restore capability independent of user-created ad hoc copies. Which approach should be evaluated?
constraints: The selected FSx deployment supports automatic backups.
The retention period is part of the file-system policy.
Restore testing is required.

options.text: Configure the FSx file system’s automatic backup settings and retention, then test a restore and use AWS Backup or copies for requirements beyond that native window.
Use an S3 bucket lifecycle rule because FSx automatic backups are customer-managed S3 objects in the application account.
Use a route table because backup retention is selected by the path from clients to the file system.
Disable automatic backups and rely on file-system replication alone because replication is always a point-in-time backup.

feedback.Reason: FSx provides service-specific automatic backup settings for supported file systems, while broader retention may require AWS Backup or copies.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The file system’s backup configuration controls automatic backups and retention within the service’s supported limits. A restore test validates that the backup is usable.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner configures the required window, checks backup status, performs a restore into an isolated target, and maps longer retention to a separate control.
Details.errorCorrection: Service-managed FSx backup storage is not governed by an application S3 lifecycle rule, route tables do not set retention, and replication is not automatically the same as backup history.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Native automatic backups simplify operations but have service-specific limits and do not eliminate the need for independent recovery copies or restore procedures.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: FSx automatic backups are configured through FSx controls rather than as ordinary application-managed S3 objects.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Route tables control packet paths and do not configure backup retention.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Replication and backup solve different recovery objectives; replication alone does not establish retained historical recovery points.

items.prompt: Application logs in CloudWatch Logs must be searchable for 30 days and then removed to meet a data-minimization policy. Which configuration is appropriate?
constraints: Logs are in CloudWatch log groups.
The retention period is a log-group policy.
The team wants automatic deletion after the period.

options.text: Set the required retention period on each CloudWatch Logs log group and verify that new groups receive the intended policy through governance or deployment controls.
Set an EC2 security-group timeout because CloudWatch log retention follows network connection state.
Use CloudTrail event history retention because CloudWatch Logs automatically inherits CloudTrail’s retention setting.
Delete the log group immediately after every incident because retention cannot be configured for CloudWatch Logs.

feedback.Reason: CloudWatch Logs supports a retention setting at the log-group level for automatic deletion of older log events.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A log group’s retention setting controls how long log events are retained; it is separate from log delivery, metric alarms, and CloudTrail event-history settings.
Details.scenarioApplication: The platform sets retention during log-group provisioning, detects groups without the policy, and exports only records that require longer governed retention.
Details.errorCorrection: Security groups do not manage log retention, CloudTrail history is a separate service setting, and immediate deletion loses the required search window.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Short retention reduces cost and exposure but can remove evidence needed for investigations; longer retention should be placed in a governed archive when required.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Security-group connection state does not determine CloudWatch Logs event retention.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: CloudTrail and CloudWatch Logs have separate retention controls and are not automatically coupled.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: CloudWatch Logs log groups support configurable retention periods.

items.prompt: Audit logs must remain available for seven years, while CloudTrail delivery should continue even if the logging account is compromised. Which architecture is most appropriate?
constraints: The organization has a dedicated log archive account.
Long-term retention is required.
The archive must be protected from ordinary workload deletion.

options.text: Create an organization or account trail that delivers logs to a dedicated S3 log archive, apply tightly scoped access and lifecycle retention, and add immutability controls when required.
Keep logs only in CloudTrail event history because it automatically provides seven-year immutable retention for every account.
Store logs on an ephemeral instance volume because local disks cannot be reached by an attacker using AWS APIs.
Disable log validation because validation prevents lifecycle rules from expiring old audit records.

feedback.Reason: CloudTrail trails deliver durable audit records to a governed destination where retention, access, and immutability can be designed explicitly.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A trail can deliver events to S3; organization trails and a separate log archive account reduce account-local tampering risk. S3 lifecycle and Object Lock can address retention requirements.
Details.scenarioApplication: Security centralizes delivery, limits archive access, monitors trail health, and tests that protected records remain available for investigations.
Details.errorCorrection: Event history is not a seven-year archive, instance disks are not a durable audit repository, and log validation is an integrity control rather than a lifecycle blocker.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Centralized immutable archives improve evidence durability but add cross-account policy, key, retention, and operational ownership requirements.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: CloudTrail event history is not the design for a seven-year immutable archive.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Ephemeral instance storage is not durable or centrally governed audit evidence.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Log file validation helps detect tampering and does not replace or inherently prevent retention policies.

items.prompt: A platform has hot customer data, regulated records, backups, and disposable processing output. What is the strongest first step for a lifecycle design?
constraints: Each class has a different business owner.
Retention and deletion obligations differ.
The design must be enforceable by AWS controls.

options.text: Define data classes, owners, retention and deletion rules, recovery objectives, and legal-hold exceptions first; then map each class to service-native lifecycle and protection controls.
Choose the lowest-cost storage class for every object first and infer retention from its storage price.
Apply one account-wide deletion schedule because separate data owners make lifecycle governance impossible.
Encrypt every record with a separate key and treat key deletion as the complete retention policy.

feedback.Reason: Retention architecture starts with data classification and obligations, then selects controls that enforce each class’s lifecycle and recovery needs.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Classification connects ownership, retention, deletion, legal hold, storage tier, backup, and restore requirements to the right service controls.
Details.scenarioApplication: The platform documents a control matrix and implements scoped lifecycle rules, backup plans, Object Lock, and log retention by class.
Details.errorCorrection: Storage price does not define obligations, one deletion schedule ignores data differences, and encryption-key deletion is not equivalent to governed data deletion.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Class-based lifecycle design requires more ownership and tagging discipline but prevents accidental deletion, over-retention, and mismatched recovery behavior.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Cost is one lifecycle input, not the basis for retention or legal obligations.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: An account-wide schedule cannot safely govern data with different retention classes.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Key lifecycle and data lifecycle are related but not interchangeable controls.

items.prompt: A product owner asks to reduce all backup retention to cut cost, but the service has a seven-day recovery point objective and a 30-day operational recovery requirement. What should the architect do?
constraints: The recovery objectives are approved requirements.
Backups are the primary operational recovery path.
Cost optimization is still required.

options.text: Keep enough retained recovery points to meet the stated RPO and recovery window, then optimize through tiering, deduplication where supported, scoped backup classes, and deletion of only eligible copies.
Delete all backups after seven days because the RPO is seven days and RPO defines how long data must be retained.
Increase retention indefinitely because longer retention always improves RTO and has no governance or cost trade-off.
Replace backups with read replicas because a replica is a historical recovery point with the same retention semantics.

feedback.Reason: Retention must satisfy recovery objectives first, while cost optimization removes only copies that are outside approved recovery and compliance requirements.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: RPO describes acceptable data loss, RTO describes restoration time, and retention describes how far back a usable recovery point must remain. They are related but distinct.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner models recovery scenarios, preserves the 30-day window, and applies lower-cost tiers or class-specific policies to reduce spend safely.
Details.errorCorrection: A seven-day RPO does not imply seven-day retention, indefinite retention adds cost and governance burden, and replicas are not historical backups.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Longer retention improves historical recovery but increases cost, privacy exposure, and deletion obligations; the design must make the trade-off explicit.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: RPO measures acceptable loss, not the required age of the oldest recoverable copy.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Indefinite retention is not automatically better and can violate cost, privacy, or deletion requirements.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A read replica supports availability or read scaling and does not provide the same historical retention as backups.
